query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a moderate level of Zr (x = 0.05 nominal) to the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance its mechanical performance under long-term mechanical loading and room-temperature creep while still providing improved corrosion resistance compared to the Zr-free alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (x = 0) with a ~70% FCC-dominant FCC + ordered B2 dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce Zr alloying at a nominal composition of x = 0.05 into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy using the same processing route (cold-crucible/vacuum melting under Ar with remelts).
generation.conditions: Testing conducted under the conditions used for the original study: microhardness using a 0.981 N load for 15 s; room-temperature compression on 3 mm × 6 mm cylinders at a strain rate of 1 × 10^-3 s^-1 to a strain of 0.3; nanoindentation creep with a 10 mN peak load and 100 s hold time at various loading rates; and corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl (immersion for 30 min, potentiodynamic polarization from -0.8 to 1.5 V at 1 mV/s, and EIS from 10^-2 to 10^4 Hz).
generation.structural_mediator: Moderate Zr addition (x = 0.05) is expected to cause lattice distortion within the FCC/B2 matrix and promote the formation of finely dispersed or discontinuously networked Ni7Zr2 precipitates that nucleate at phase boundaries, while only slightly reducing the B2 volume fraction.
generation.mechanism: The moderate Zr content leads to solid-solution strengthening through lattice distortion and enhances dispersion/precipitation strengthening via the formation of fine, coherent or semi-coherent Ni7Zr2 precipitates. These precipitates impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thus reducing creep and increasing hardness, yield strength, and compressive strength. Although excessive Zr (x = 0.1) may form a continuous Zr-rich network that favors corrosion resistance by stabilizing a protective passive film (possibly ZrO2), the moderate level at x = 0.05 appears to offer a better overall balance between mechanical strength and corrosion resistance for applications demanding both.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Zr-free alloy, the x = 0.05 alloy is predicted to exhibit higher hardness, yield strength, and compressive strength along with reduced room-temperature creep deformation. While corrosion resistance might not be as high as with x = 0.1, it will still be improved compared to the baseline alloy, providing a balanced enhancement in performance for conditions involving extreme temperature fluctuations, sustained mechanical loads, room-temperature creep, and corrosion exposure.
generation.baseline: The starting x = 0 AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with measured properties of yield strength ~705 MPa, compressive strength ~1183 MPa, corrosion current density ~0.1 μA/cm², pitting potential ~320 mV, corrosion rate ~0.00116 mm/year, and charge-transfer resistance ~2600 Ω·cm².
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to the as-cast, high-purity AlCoCrFeNi2.1 system processed under Ar via cold-crucible/vacuum melting and remelted at least five times. Mechanical testing is at room temperature under specified compression and nanoindentation creep conditions, and corrosion testing is in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. It is specific to nominal Zr contents around x = 0.05; higher Zr content (x = 0.1) may offer superior corrosion resistance but at the expense of mechanical properties due to phase coarsening and embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact trade-off between the enhanced mechanical properties and potential minor compromises in corrosion resistance at x = 0.05 compared to x = 0.1 is uncertain. Additional detailed quantitative studies are required to optimize the Zr level for the specific application requirements of fasteners under combined mechanical and corrosive conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys with Zr additions at x = 0 (control), x = 0.01, x = 0.05, and x = 0.1 under the same casting conditions. Characterize the microstructures using XRD, SEM/EDS, and TEM/SAED to observe phase evolution and precipitate morphology. Conduct microhardness tests, room-temperature compression tests, and nanoindentation creep experiments to assess mechanical performance. Perform potentiodynamic polarization and EIS measurements after 30 min immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl to evaluate corrosion resistance.
measurements: Phase and precipitate morphology from XRD, SEM/EDS, and TEM/SAED.
Microhardness values under a 0.981 N load for 15 s.
Yield strength and compressive strength from room-temperature compression tests.
Creep resistance metrics from nanoindentation creep (displacement and stress exponent n).
Corrosion parameters: Icorr, Ecorr, Epit from potentiodynamic polarization; charge-transfer resistance (Rct) from EIS, along with post-corrosion SEM/EDS analyses.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the x = 0.05 alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in hardness, yield strength, compressive strength, and reduced creep deformation relative to the x = 0 control (or shows degraded mechanical performance), or if the corrosion resistance is not improved relative to the control under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is rejected.
